RULEMAKING TO UPDATE                                                    §                PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION

IN THE ERCOT REGION                                                     §

        GUADALUPE VALLEY ELECTRIC COOPERATIVE, INC.’S COMMENTS
                ON STAFF’S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF
             AMENDMENTS TO §25.192 AND §25.193 AND NEW §25.252


                                                    TABLE OF CONTENTS
I.    The Commission Should Not Replace the 4CP Methodology with 12CP, and GVEC’s Own
      System Data Confirms That 12CP Would Increase Costs to Its Cooperative Members
      (§25.192). ................................................................................................................................ 3
II.   GVEC Supports the Proposal’s Direct Assignment of Transmission Costs to Large Loads
      (New §25.252 and §25.192).................................................................................................... 4

     Internal Cross-Reference (§25.192 and §25.193). .................................................................. 7

                                                                   Page 1
        Guadalupe Valley Electric Cooperative, Inc. (“GVEC”) respectfully submits these

comments in response to the Public Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission”) Staff’s (“Staff”)

proposal for publication of amendments to 16 Texas Administrative Code (“TAC”) §25.192 and

§25.193 and new §25.252, which the Commission approved for publication at its July 9, 2026 open

meeting. GVEC is a Texas electric cooperative that owns and operates transmission and

distribution assets and provides retail electric service to its members in its statutorily authorized

service area. GVEC participates in the ERCOT wholesale market and pays wholesale transmission

costs on behalf of its members. The proposal directs that comments be filed by August 11, 2026;

accordingly, these comments are timely.


                                            Comments
       GVEC is a Non-Opt-In Entity (“NOIE”), and its board of directors maintains the exclusive

right to set its retail rates for all classes of customers. GVEC incorporates by reference the

comments of Texas Electric Cooperatives, Inc. (“TEC”) and will not repeat the arguments made

in those comments. Although GVEC is not subject to the Commission’s jurisdiction with respect

to its retail rates, GVEC follows cost-causation principles in its own rate design and has a strong

interest in ensuring that the wholesale transmission cost recovery framework reflects those

principles. Because GVEC is both a non-IOU transmission service provider (“TSP”) and a non-

IOU distribution service provider (“DSP”), amended §25.192 and the TSP tariff requirements of

new §25.252 apply to GVEC, while §25.193 — which by its terms applies only to investor-owned

DSPs — does not.




                                               Page 2
       I.     The Commission Should Not Replace the 4CP Methodology with 12CP, and
             GVEC’s Own System Data Confirms That 12CP Would Increase Costs to Its
                               Cooperative Members (§25.192).
   GVEC continues to support retaining the existing four coincident peak (“4CP”) methodology.

Transmission planning in ERCOT is driven primarily by the need to reliably serve load during

forecasted summer peak conditions and potential contingency events, and in ERCOT the highest

demand has consistently occurred during the summer months of June through September. Because

the system is planned for the summer peak, costs should be allocated on the same basis. Assigning

costs using twelve coincident peaks (“12CP”) unmoors cost allocation from the conditions that

actually drive transmission investment, and it does so without correcting the structural inequity

that Senate Bill 6 was enacted to address.


   GVEC’s objection is not merely theoretical. GVEC analyzed ERCOT TDSP-level 15-minute

interval data for 2020 through 2025 and compared each distribution system’s share of ERCOT

transmission cost of service (“TCOS”) under 4CP against the shares that result under alternative

methodologies, including 12CP. The results are consistent and adverse to GVEC’s members: in

every year studied, moving from 4CP to 12CP increases GVEC’s share of ERCOT transmission

cost — by approximately 10% to 18% each year relative to 4CP (a 13.6% relative increase in

2025). Applied to GVEC’s 2025 transmission cost of service of approximately $36.7 million, a

13.6% increase equates to roughly $5 million per year in additional transmission cost borne by

GVEC’s members.


   GVEC’s analysis also shows that the burden grows as measurement periods are added:

GVEC’s cost share rises monotonically as the methodology moves from 4CP to 5CP, 6CP, 7CP,

and 12CP. In short, the methodology change shifts cost onto systems like GVEC’s without any

corresponding change in the burden those members place on the transmission system. GVEC’s


                                             Page 3
 internal study concluded that 4CP remains the most stable and lowest-cost methodology for GVEC

across all years and rate classes, and that no alternative examined matches 4CP’s balance of cost

stability, fairness, and grid-supportive behavior.


   Critically, 12CP does not solve the problem Senate Bill 6 targets. The core inequity in the

current framework is that sophisticated large loads can and do curtail consumption during

predictable coincident-peak intervals, shifting cost to customers who cannot. Adding measurement

periods does not eliminate that incentive; large loads will adapt their curtailment behavior to any

new measurement window over time. The durable and appropriately targeted fix is to assign large-

load-driven costs directly to large loads, which Staff’s proposal now does through new §25.252

and the minimum billing demand provisions discussed below. Because those provisions address

the cost-shift directly, the blunt reallocation effected by 12CP is unnecessary and works to the

detriment of GVEC’s members. Allocating costs on a basis other than the summer peak that drives

transmission investment is also in tension with the requirements of PURA §36.003 that rates be

just, reasonable, and not unreasonably preferential or discriminatory.


   If the Commission nonetheless proceeds with 12CP, GVEC’s data underscores why the large-

load direct-assignment provisions must be adopted in their strongest form. Those provisions are

what prevent the cost increase that 12CP imposes on cooperatives from being borne by residential

and small-commercial members rather than by the large loads whose growth drives new

transmission investment.


      II.     GVEC Supports the Proposal’s Direct Assignment of Transmission Costs to
                             Large Loads (New §25.252 and §25.192).
   Direct assignment of transmission costs to large loads is the most effective way to address the

concerns underlying Senate Bill 6 with the least disruption to residential and small-commercial


                                               Page 4
 customers. The steady growth of large loads makes it increasingly important that transmission

costs driven by that growth not be socialized across all ratepayers. GVEC therefore supports the

core of the proposal, which converts the direct-assignment principles GVEC advocated in Project

No. 58484 into binding tariff requirements.


    GVEC supports new §25.252(c), which requires each TSP and IOU-DSP tariff to obligate large

load customers to post financial security, to pay contribution in aid of construction (“CIAC”) for

both transmission and distribution interconnection costs as a direct cash payment, and to execute

an interconnection agreement with a term of not less than 20 years, and which prohibits any

allowance for CIAC. Interconnection allowances convert a direct, load-specific cost into a shared

system cost. For purpose-built interconnections serving large loads of 75 MW or more, most of

the associated transmission investment is built for, and located where, that individual load chooses

to site; the “shared benefit” premise that historically justified allowances does not hold at that scale

and specificity. Eliminating allowances and requiring CIAC restores the “but-for” causal

connection between the large load and the investment its interconnection triggers, and it improves

siting incentives by ensuring that large loads — sophisticated commercial actors with substantial

capital and bargaining power — bear the true cost of where and how they interconnect.


    For the same reasons, GVEC supports the requirement that non-refundable interconnection

fees paid under §25.194, and financial security forfeited under §25.194, be used to offset the TSP’s

transmission revenue requirement. Flowing those large-load-specific payments through as a

reduction to the revenue requirement ensures that other customers are not asked to subsidize costs

caused by, and recovered from, large loads.




                                                Page 5
    GVEC also supports the large load minimum billing demand established in §25.193(d) and

§25.252(e). Transmission is sized to serve a large load’s full contracted capacity at any time, and

a minimum billing demand set at contracted peak demand correctly attributes cost causation and

resolves the mismatch that arises when a large load curtails during measured peak intervals. GVEC

likewise supports the requirement that billing commence at the level of available service when

capacity is made available, irrespective of whether the large load has energized or is fully using

that capacity, because the transmission system must be sized and ready to serve the reserved

capacity regardless of the load’s actual utilization. Because transmission assets are long-lived —

typically 30 to 40 years — and their costs are recovered over decades, a firm commitment period

ensures that a meaningful portion of the capital triggered by large load growth is recovered from

those loads before they can exit the market, reducing stranded-cost risk to remaining customers. A

minimum billing demand also produces a more authentic demand-response signal driven by energy

prices rather than transmission-bill avoidance.


   GVEC’s support for a robust minimum billing demand is reinforced by its own cost data. As

shown in Section I, the shift to 12CP increases the transmission costs GVEC must recover on

behalf of its members by 10% to 18% each year; the larger that burden, the more it matters that

costs driven by large-load growth are recovered from the large loads that cause them rather than

socialized onto members who largely cannot avoid the peaks on which the system is planned.

Setting the minimum billing demand at the greater of contracted peak, NCP, or 12CP demand —

at or near 100% of contracted capacity — maximizes that recovery and is therefore the level most

protective of GVEC’s residential and small-commercial members. The independent modeling filed




                                              Page 6
 by the Texas Energy Buyers Alliance in this proceeding 1 is consistent with GVEC’s position: it

confirms that higher minimum-billing-demand levels provide progressively greater protection to

existing customers.


       III.    The Commission Should Confirm Protections for Non-Opt-In Entities and
                     Correct an Internal Cross-Reference (§25.192 and §25.193).
    GVEC does not oppose the requirement in §25.192(f)(1)(A) that non-IOU DSPs provide

ERCOT timely access to settlement-quality meter data for each large load customer, but it asks the

Commission to make the obligation workable and bounded. The Commission should define

“timely” and “settlement-quality,” align the requirement with existing ERCOT metering and

registration processes rather than a new parallel data feed, and provide confidentiality protection

for competitively sensitive large-load and member data submitted to ERCOT. The Commission

should also confirm on the record that this data obligation is limited to what is necessary to perform

the 12CP adjustment and does not expand the Commission’s jurisdiction over GVEC’s retail rate

design or class structure.


    GVEC further requests that the Commission correct an internal cross-reference that is

unworkable for NOIEs as drafted. Section 25.192(f)(1)(B) directs ERCOT to adjust each DSP’s

12CP load — including each non-IOU DSP’s — by the difference between each large load

customer’s “large load minimum billing demand” and its measured 12CP. But the defined term

“large load minimum billing demand” is established by reference to §25.193, which applies only



1
 The independent modeling referenced herein is the transmission cost of service analysis prepared
by J. Pollock, Incorporated and filed by the Texas Energy Buyers Alliance in this proceeding. See
Void letter for item 11 and Large Load Minimum Billing Demand Study (July 30, 2026). GVEC
cites that analysis solely for its quantitative findings regarding the relationship between minimum-
billing-demand levels and cost recovery from existing customers and does not adopt the filing
party’s policy recommendations.


                                               Page 7
 to investor-owned DSPs. For a non-IOU DSP’s large load, no §25.193 value necessarily exists,

leaving the wholesale adjustment mechanism undefined for cooperatives. GVEC recommends that

the Commission clarify that, for a non-IOU DSP, the large load minimum billing demand used for

the §25.192(f)(1)(B) adjustment is established from the large load’s contracted peak demand or

available service under §25.194 and the interconnection agreement required by §25.252, applying

the same “greater-of” measure the rule uses for investor-owned DSPs, while expressly preserving

the authority of the NOIE’s governing board over how it recovers those costs at retail. This

clarification makes the rule internally consistent and administrable; it does not expand the

Commission’s jurisdiction, because the wholesale adjustment can proceed without the

Commission setting GVEC’s retail rates.


   GVEC also asks the Commission to confirm that the requirement to update class allocation

factor values annually applies only to investor-owned DSPs, consistent with the applicability of

§25.193, and to retain the existing provisions allowing non-IOU TSPs to use the cash-flow method

and to determine return based on actual debt service and a reasonable coverage ratio. Finally,

GVEC requests that the Commission ensure the transition provisions afford adequate lead time —

both for ERCOT to publish the first-year 12CP determinations far enough in advance for

cooperatives to budget, and for the tariff compliance filings required after adoption.


                    IV.     Responses to the Commission’s Specific Questions.
Question 1 (differentiated values). GVEC does not recommend different minimum-billing-

demand values for large loads with different contracted peak or NCP demands. Using contracted

peak demand will already scale the charge to the individual load and will most accurately represent

the load’s burden on the transmission system for the point at which its transmission needs were

studied. Using contracted peak demand will also discipline large loads to more accurately forecast


                                              Page 8
 their power needs. Bespoke values would invite potential gaming and administrative complexity

without improving cost causation.


Question 2 (duration). GVEC supports a firm term — the proposed 20 years (240 consecutive

payments) — and opposes phasing the minimum demand down over the period. Transmission

assets have useful lives of 30 to 40 years and are recovered over decades, so a firm 20-year term

ensures that a meaningful portion of the capital triggered by a large load is recovered before that

load can exit. A phase-down would reintroduce cost-shifting onto GVEC’s members before that

long-lived capital is recovered. The modeling in the record is consistent with this position,

indicating that a minimum demand at or near 100% of contracted demand recovers large-load costs

quickly and makes a phase-down unnecessary.


Question 3 (lower measure; ratchet or weighted average). GVEC opposes basing the minimum

billing demand on any measure lower than contracted peak demand, including a ratcheted demand

or a 12CP-weighted average. A minimum keyed to a curtailing load’s 12CP would defeat the

purpose of the provision by allowing sophisticated loads to curtail out of the cost responsibility

the minimum is meant to secure — the precise loophole the reform is intended to close. The

modeling in the record is consistent with GVEC’s position, confirming that diluting the minimum

below roughly 75% of contracted demand shifts transmission costs back onto other customer

classes, including GVEC’s members.


Question 4 (large computational loads). GVEC supports separate rate treatment for large

computational loads (such as data centers and cryptocurrency facilities) where that treatment rests

on demonstrable differences in cost causation or usage — for example, distinct load shapes,

flexibility, power quality requirements, or interconnection cost profiles — rather than on the



                                              Page 9
 identity of the customer. Any such classification must satisfy PURA §36.003, which prohibits rates

that are unreasonably preferential, prejudicial, or discriminatory, and the Commission should

recognize that class design for a NOIE remains a matter for the cooperative’s governing board.


Question 5 (definition of transmission interconnection costs). GVEC supports broadening the

definition of “transmission interconnection costs” to include transmission projects recommended

at the conclusion of a batch study to serve the transmission capacity needs of a particular load.

Where a study identifies transmission required to serve a specific load’s capacity needs, those costs

are load-caused and should be directly assignable rather than socialized, consistent with cost-

causation principles. GVEC asks only that the definition be drawn precisely enough to avoid

sweeping in genuinely shared network upgrades that benefit the system as a whole.


Question 6 (reserved capacity in planning and resource adequacy). GVEC supports reflecting

reserved-but-unenergized capacity in resource adequacy reports and assessments and in

transmission planning studies. If a large load is billed on reserved capacity and available service

under §25.252, planning and resource adequacy processes should recognize that capacity so that

studies remain accurate and existing customers are not exposed to stranded or under-recovered

costs.


                                          V.      Conclusion
GVEC appreciates the opportunity to provide these comments. GVEC respectfully urges the

Commission to retain the 4CP methodology, and — should it proceed with 12CP over GVEC’s

objection — to adopt the large-load direct-assignment provisions in their strongest form, to correct

the cross-reference so the minimum billing demand mechanism is administrable for non-opt-in

entities, and to confirm the protections for cooperatives described above. These measures represent




                                               Page 10
 the most targeted and equitable path to implement Senate Bill 6 while protecting the residential

and small-commercial members who cannot avoid the peaks on which transmission is planned.



Dated: August 10, 2026.
                                                Respectfully submitted,



                                                Amanda Frazier
                                                State Bar No. 24032198
                                                General Counsel & Chief Regulatory Officer,
                                                GVEC
                                                P.O. Box 118
                                                Gonzales, Texas 78629

                                   EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
    OF COMMENTS OF GUADALUPE VALLEY ELECTRIC COOPERATIVE, INC.


GVEC’s substantive recommendations are summarized as follows:


•   Retain the 4CP methodology (§25.192). The Commission should retain 4CP. GVEC’s

    analysis of 2020–2025 ERCOT interval data shows that 12CP increases GVEC’s share of

    ERCOT transmission cost every year — roughly 10% to 18% relative to 4CP (about $5 million

    per year applied to GVEC’s 2025 cost of service) — without curing the large-load cost-shift

    that Senate Bill 6 targets. 4CP aligns cost allocation with the summer peak on which

    transmission is planned.


•   Rely on direct large-load assignment, not a methodology change. The proposal’s large-

    load provisions, not 12CP, are the durable fix for cost-shifting. If the Commission adopts

    12CP, it should adopt those provisions in their strongest form to prevent 12CP’s cost increase

    from falling on residential and small-commercial members.


•   Support CIAC and the prohibition on interconnection allowances (§25.252(c)). GVEC

    supports requiring large loads to pay contribution in aid of construction as a direct cash

    payment, prohibiting interconnection allowances, and requiring a 20-year interconnection

    agreement, and supports offsetting the TSP revenue requirement with non-refundable

    interconnection fees and forfeited security.



                                              Page 12
 •   Support the large load minimum billing demand and available-service billing

    (§25.193(d), §25.252(e)). GVEC supports the using loads’ contracted peak demand, billing at

    the level of available service irrespective of energization, and a firm 20-year term. Because

    12CP increases the transmission cost GVEC’s members must recover, setting the minimum at

    or near 100% of contracted capacity — the level most protective of existing customers — is

    especially important for GVEC.


•   Oppose any dilution of the minimum billing demand (Questions 2 and 3). GVEC supports

    a firm 20-year term and opposes phase-downs, ratchets, or 12CP-weighted averages, which

    would shift cost back onto GVEC’s members before long-lived transmission capital is

    recovered. The J. Pollock modeling in the record confirms that diluting the minimum below

    roughly 75% of contracted demand shifts cost onto other customer classes.


•   Correct the §25.192(f)(1)(B) cross-reference for non-opt-in entities. Because the “large

    load minimum billing demand” is defined by reference to §25.193 (which applies only to IOU

    DSPs), the wholesale 12CP adjustment is undefined for NOIE large loads. The Commission

    should clarify that the value is set from contracted peak/available service under §25.194 and

    §25.252, while preserving the NOIE board’s authority over retail recovery.


•   Provide guardrails on the NOIE meter-data requirement (§25.192(f)(1)(A)). GVEC does

    not oppose providing large-load meter data but requests defined terms, confidentiality

    protection, alignment with existing ERCOT processes, and confirmation that the requirement

    does not expand jurisdiction over GVEC’s retail rates.


•   Confine annual allocation-factor updates to IOU DSPs and preserve non-IOU methods.

    The annual allocation-factor-update duty should apply only to investor-owned DSPs, and the



                                            Page 13
 Commission should retain the cash-flow method and debt-service-coverage return for non-

IOU TSPs, and afford adequate transition lead time.

                    IV.     Responses to the Commission's Specific Questions.
Question 1 (differentiated values). GVEC does not recommend different minimum-billing-

demand values for large loads with different contracted peak or NCP demands. Using contracted

peak demand will already scale the charge to the individual load and will most accurately represent

the load's burden on the transmission system for the point at which its transmission needs were

studied. Using contracted peak demand will also discipline large loads to more accurately forecast



                                              Page 8
 their power needs. Bespoke values would invite potential gaming and administrative complexity

without improving cost causation.


Question 2 (duration). GVEC supports a firm term - the proposed 20 years (240 consecutive

payments) - and opposes phasing the minimum demand down over the period. Transmission

assets have useful lives of 30 to 40 years and are recovered over decades, so a firm 20-year term

ensures that a meaningful portion of the capital triggered by a large load is recovered before that

load can exit. A phase-down would reintroduce cost-shifting onto GVEC's members before that

long-lived capital is recovered. The modeling in the record is consistent with this position,

indicating that a minimum demand at or near 100% ofcontracted demand recovers large-load costs

quickly and makes a phase-down unnecessary.


Question 3 (lower measure; ratchet or weighted average). GVEC opposes basing the minimum

billing demand on any measure lower than contracted peak demand, including a ratcheted demand

or a 12CP-weighted average. A minimum keyed to a curtailing load' s 12CP would defeat the

purpose of the provision by allowing sophisticated loads to curtail out of the cost responsibility

the minimum is meant to secure - the precise loophole the reform is intended to close. The

modeling in the record is consistent with GVEC's position, confirming that diluting the minimum

below roughly 75% of contracted demand shifts transmission costs back onto other customer

classes, including GVEC's members.


Question 4 (large computational loads). GVEC supports separate rate treatment for large

computational loads (such as data centers and cryptocurrency facilities) where that treatment rests

on demonstrable differences in cost causation or usage - for example, distinct load shapes,

flexibility, power quality requirements, or interconnection cost profiles - rather than on the



                                              Page 9
 identity ofthe customer. Any such classification must satisfy PURA §36.003, which prohibits rates

that are unreasonably preferential, prejudicial, or discriminatory, and the Commission should

recognize that class design for a NOIE remains a matter for the cooperative' s governing board.


Question 5 (definition of transmission interconnection costs). GVEC supports broadening the

definition of "transmission interconnection costs" to include transmission proj ects recommended

at the conclusion of a batch study to serve the transmission capacity needs of a particular load.

Where a study identifies transmission required to serve a specific load' s capacity needs, those costs

are load-caused and should be directly assignable rather than socialized, consistent with cost-

causation principles. GVEC asks only that the definition be drawn precisely enough to avoid

sweeping in genuinely shared network upgrades that benefit the system as a whole.


Question 6 (reserved capacity in planning and resource adequacy). (NEC supports reflecting

reserved-but-unenergized capacity in resource adequacy reports and assessments and in

transmission planning studies. If a large load is billed on reserved capacity and available service

under §25.252, planning and resource adequacy processes should recognize that capacity so that

studies remain accurate and existing customers are not exposed to stranded or under-recovered

costs.
